Now, based on Time's profile, which is of course all I know about Hannah, it doesn't seem to me like she's some ideologue who rejects AI on principle. It's that she has specific concerns with how it's used in her field, which she understandably feels like she has some ground-level lived experience insight into. Time writes, Drummond helped nurses at 17 facilities in the HCA hospital system, including her own, win AI protections in their most recent contract, including a provision requiring Hospitals to give registered nurses a say in how new technologies related to patient care are implemented. Drummond points to concerns that nurses have had where the improper use of AI has not only been not helpful but actively harmful. One example she gave was of an AI tool that was designed to automate shift handoffs that had assigned a patient with COVID alongside another who was immunocompromised, which created Obviously big risks for the immunocompromised patient. Drummond Time writes doesn't want to ban AI from hospitals but says there need to be strict controls around its use. She says, everything that reaches patients in healthcare has gone through rigorous testing and has proven to be safe, effective, and free from harming us. Nathaniel Whittemore, "The Week the AI Story Shifted," The AI Daily Brief, May 8 2026.

Whittemore focused less on the novelty of autonomous looping itself and more on what happens when this capability becomes reliable enough to integrate into ordinary workflows. He quoted developers who had agents running overnight on technical problems, sometimes for more than a dozen hours at a time. The implication was not merely convenience. It was a change in the shape of knowledge work.

One part of the discussion that stood out was his distinction between building a system and operating a system. He described using GPT-5.5 to reason through whether one of his own projects was appropriate for Slash Goal. The project involved turning podcast episodes into structured knowledge assets for teams. The model reportedly argued that the system architecture itself was a standard coding project, but the daily processing pipeline was a strong candidate for persistent goal execution. That distinction matters.

Slash Goal appears best suited for tasks that are persistent, inspectable, and verifiable. The agent needs a stable objective and some way to evaluate progress. A coding task with test suites fits naturally into that shape. A repeated content transformation pipeline also fits. A vague request like "make this better" does not.

Whittemore also emphasized something many people overlook when discussing autonomous agents. The bottleneck is often not the model. It is the framing of the work. He argued that weak prompts make Slash Goal behave like a normal chatbot session stretched over a longer period. The more effective approach was what he called meta prompting.

His suggested workflow was recursive. First, ask another model to research the /goal feature itself. Then ask it to examine the project you want to automate. Then ask it to generate several candidate persistent-goal prompts optimized for that project. Only after that do you hand the resulting specification to the long-running agent.

That approach treats prompting less like issuing commands and more like designing operational scaffolding. The human defines constraints, evaluation criteria, formats, and boundaries. The agent handles iteration inside that frame.

Whittemore connected this trend to a broader transition happening across the AI industry. He argued that the field is entering a "harness engineering" phase. Raw model intelligence already exceeds what many organizations can operationalize. The real work now involves memory systems, orchestration layers, review pipelines, persistent agents, and tooling that keeps models aligned with long-running objectives.

Seen through that lens, Slash Goal is not just another coding feature. It is part of a larger attempt to turn language models from reactive assistants into ongoing computational labor. The important question is no longer whether a model can generate a clever response. It is whether a system can sustain directed effort over time without losing coherence.

That changes the economics of AI usage. If agents can remain active for hours or days while incrementally advancing toward a goal, token consumption scales in a different direction. More importantly, the role of the human shifts. The valuable skill stops being rapid-fire prompting and becomes the design of environments where autonomous work can proceed safely and productively.

I heard this discussed on The AI Daily Brief — snipped audio and transcript, 09:06. The discussion included substantial skepticism about the interpretation: this particular incident may have been a rare anomaly or a training artifact, and the evidence does not establish a deliberate backdoor.

My takeaway is that the explanation for this incident and the broader possibility are separate questions. Ever since DeepSeek became a thing, I’ve been considering whether open-weight models could be tainted and become a vector for exploitation and influence campaigns.
We will eventually need to operate as though that risk is real.

I think it’s quite possible, perhaps likely, that the U.S. government will eventually require government agencies and recipients of government funding to establish the provenance of any open-weight models those institutions use, including whether their training sources are approved. I’m thinking of something analogous to how accessibility requirements apply through the ADA and standards such as WCAG. That’s a prediction about where policy could go. Satya Nadella’s push toward model sovereignty and Microsoft’s move into open-weight models for fine-tuning look to me like signals in that direction.

Person/Nathaniel Whittemore/Pod, with guest Person/Nufar Gaspar. Gaspar describes how to brief an AI tool, ask it to challenge your thinking, and check that its draft fits the intended reader.
27:22 — Think Before You Open The AI Tool
Gaspar's first habit: "you have to know what you're thinking before you open the tool." Take a walk or read until you have a view of your own, however messy.

Then brain-dump to the tool by dictation: what you heard, what worries you, what you think, and what you are sure you don't want. Let the tool find the structure. She says this episode started with 15 minutes of her talking to an AI tool that way.
She calls this the step people skip that has the largest effect on everything after it.
28:13 — Tell AI How Hard To Challenge Your Thinking

Tell the model how confident you are and how hard to push back, because it is built to agree with you. Her example: "I'm about 60% sure the problem is onboarding. Push back hard before you agree with me."
Before starting, decide who the audience is and what you want them to feel or do, with standards for length, format and tone. That target also gives you something to check the result against.
28:58 — Push AI Beyond Its Average First Answer

The first answer is the most probable one, and often the most average. Ask for six directions that differ in approach, angle or structure, including some borrowed from other fields, and have the tool argue for each.
29:46 — Choose AI Interception Points Before Polish Creates Sunk Cost
"Here's what I need, go and do it end to end" looks most efficient and does the most damage: a polished draft creates sunk cost, and people ship it rather than return to the argument.
30:20 — Set Strategic Checkpoints Before AI Does the Work
Decide in advance where you will step in — the outline, the first section, the narrative, the draft — at the points where changing course costs least.
